questionText: A chat app saves a message ("Movie tonight?") and, a minute later, Aman reacts with a thumbs-up. SQL keeps messages and reactions in two tables; MongoDB keeps the reaction inside the message document. How many writes does each side need for these two events?
option1: SQL: 2 inserts. MongoDB: only 1 insert in total, because reactions are saved together with the message
option2: SQL: 1 insert, because the reaction goes into the same row as the message. MongoDB: 2 separate writes
option3: SQL: 2 inserts. MongoDB: 1 insert, then 1 update. Both need 2 writes, so this case is a tie
option4: SQL: 3 writes, because of the foreign key check. MongoDB: 1 write, because documents need no keys
correctOptionExplanation: The reaction arrives later, so MongoDB updates the existing document instead of inserting a new one: 2 writes on each side. Plain writes do not separate the two; the later cases do.

questionText: Zoya opens the chat and must see message 101 together with its 3 reactions. What does each side hand back to the app?
option1: SQL: 1 row that holds all 3 reactions in a single column. MongoDB: 3 documents, one per reaction
option2: SQL: a JOIN returns 3 rows with the message text repeated. MongoDB: 1 document already shaped like the screen
option3: SQL: 1 row and 1 query. MongoDB: 1 document, but a second query is needed to fetch the reactions, since arrays are stored apart
option4: Both return exactly 3 rows, because MongoDB also stores every reaction as its own separate row
correctOptionExplanation: The join repeats the message text once per reaction and the app has to glue the rows back into one message. The document already contains the message and its reactions, so one read is enough.

questionText: Om sends a poll ("Which show?") with the options 7 PM and 10 PM. In SQL the poll goes into messages and the options into poll_options. What should wrap the two INSERTs so that a poll never exists without its options?
option1: A UNIQUE constraint on poll_options, so the same option text cannot be saved twice for one poll, and so the data stays consistent
option2: An index on poll_options.message_id, so that the options of a poll are found quickly later
option3: A transaction (START TRANSACTION ... COMMIT), so both inserts succeed together or neither is saved
option4: A SELECT after the inserts, to check that both rows really exist before replying to the user
correctOptionExplanation: A transaction makes the two inserts all-or-nothing (ROLLBACK if anything fails). In MongoDB the poll is one document, and a single-document insert is already all-or-nothing.

questionText: A message goes viral and 6 people react in the same second. Which is the real weakness of embedding the reactions inside the message document?
option1: Every reaction needs its own index entry, so the 6 writes become very slow one after another, which is why embedding never scales
option2: MongoDB cannot store an array of reactions inside a document, so the data has to be flattened
option3: The reactions can no longer be read together with the message text without a second query
option4: All 6 writes hit the same document, so they take turns, and it keeps growing towards the 16 MB limit
correctOptionExplanation: In SQL every reaction is a new row, so the 6 inserts run side by side. One shared document turns into a queue. Real apps keep viral reactions in their own collection and store only a count in the message.

questionText: Rahul deletes message 101, which has 2 reactions. Select ALL the true statements.
option1: In SQL, rows must be removed from both messages and reactions
option2: In SQL, both deletes should sit in one transaction, so no orphan reactions are left behind
option3: In MongoDB, a single deleteOne removes the message together with its embedded reactions
option4: In MongoDB, a second delete is needed to clean up the reactions
option5: In SQL, deleting the row from messages always deletes its reactions as well, with no foreign key or extra statement
correctOptionExplanation: SQL touches two tables (and a transaction keeps them in step). The MongoDB document holds the reactions, so deleting it removes them. SQL only cascades if you define a foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE.

questionText: Messages are sharded by chat_id across servers. The reactions table has no chat_id, so it is sharded by message_id. Where do the reactions of a chat-7 message end up, and what is the SQL fix?
option1: On the same server as the message, because shard keys are copied along. No fix is needed here
option2: Always on the same server, but reading them is slower. Fix: add an index on message_id in reactions
option3: Often on another server than the message. Fix: copy chat_id into reactions and shard by it too (co-location)
option4: Nowhere, because the insert fails. Fix: remove the shard key from messages so both tables agree
correctOptionExplanation: Reading or deleting one message now needs two servers. Copying chat_id into every child table puts a message and its children together. In MongoDB the reactions are inside the message, so they always travel with it.

questionText: The app launches voice notes (a url and a duration). The SQL data is spread over 8 shards and holds 2 billion messages. What must happen before the feature ships?
option1: SQL: nothing, new columns appear when the first voice note is inserted. MongoDB: a migration on every shard before it can store anything new
option2: SQL: a schema change (new table or columns) on every shard. MongoDB: nothing, just save documents with the new fields
option3: Both need an ALTER on every shard before release, because MongoDB documents also follow a fixed schema
option4: Both need nothing: MySQL and MongoDB both add columns or fields on demand without any change
correctOptionExplanation: A new SQL column or table has to exist on every shard first. A MongoDB document can simply carry the new fields; old documents stay as they are, and your app must cope with documents that lack them.

questionText: On her profile, Zoya sees "Which emoji do you use most?" across every chat. Which design does less work to answer it?
option1: SQL: a reactions table with an index on user reads only her rows, then groups them by emoji
option2: MongoDB: reactions live inside messages, so it reads only Zoya's reactions and skips the rest
option3: Both read the same amount of data, because the way it is stored makes no difference to the work
option4: MongoDB, because embedded documents are always faster to scan than rows in an indexed table
correctOptionExplanation: In MongoDB her reactions are scattered inside many different messages, so it opens whole messages and unwinds them. Embedding is built for one way of looking at the data (by message); other angles cost more.

questionText: Zoya changes her display name. In MongoDB her name was copied into every message she ever sent. What has to change?
option1: Only one document, because MongoDB keeps the copies of her name linked to each other
option2: Nothing, because old messages keep the name they were sent with and MongoDB cannot change them
option3: Every message she ever sent, so potentially millions of documents have to be rewritten
option4: Only her most recent message, since older messages are archived and read-only by default
correctOptionExplanation: In SQL the name lives once in users and messages point to her id, so one row changes. The MongoDB fix is the same idea: keep only her id in each message and look the name up. Copying shared data that changes is expensive.

questionText: Chats live on 2 MySQL servers, picked in the app by chat_id % 2. A third server is added and the rule becomes chat_id % 3. What happens to the existing chats?
option1: Nothing moves; only brand-new chats are placed on the third server under the new rule
option2: MySQL notices the new server and rebalances the existing data across all three by itself
option3: Each chat moves lazily, the first time it is read through the new rule, with no scripts
option4: Most of them now map to a different server, so your own scripts must copy them while users chat
correctOptionExplanation: Changing the rule remaps most chat ids (6 of 9 in the animation). Sharding by hand means you write the copy scripts and redeploy. In MongoDB, sh.addShard is enough: the balancer moves chunks in the background and mongos routes to the new place.

questionText: Select ALL the true statements about sharding in MongoDB.
option1: mongos routes each query to the shard that holds the data
option2: The config servers store which chunk lives on which shard
option3: After sh.addShard, the application code must be changed to know about the new shard
option4: The balancer moves chunks to the new shard in the background
option5: You must copy the data to the new shard yourself with scripts
correctOptionExplanation: The app talks to mongos only. The config servers hold the chunk map, and the balancer moves chunks on its own, so the app code and your scripts stay out of it.

questionText: At 2 a.m. the primary database server crashes. Who promotes a replica to primary in classic MySQL replication, and in a MongoDB replica set?
option1: MySQL: a person or an extra tool. MongoDB: the members vote and elect a new primary themselves
option2: Both promote a replica automatically within a few seconds, with no extra setup in either
option3: MySQL: the replicas vote among themselves. MongoDB: a person must promote one by hand
option4: Neither promotes anything: both stay read-only until the old primary server is repaired, which can take days
correctOptionExplanation: Classic MySQL replication has no election, so writes fail until someone promotes a replica (minutes). A MongoDB replica set elects a new primary in about 10 seconds. MySQL InnoDB Cluster can fail over automatically too, but it is extra setup.

questionText: A MongoDB replica set has 3 members and the primary dies. Why can the other two members elect a new primary?
option1: Two of three members are a majority of the voting members, and electing a primary needs a majority
option2: Any single surviving member can promote itself, because members trust each other by default
option3: They first wait for the old primary to confirm that it has stepped down, then they vote
option4: The config servers look at the replica set and pick the new primary on its behalf
correctOptionExplanation: A majority is needed so that two halves of a split network cannot both elect a primary. With only 2 members, losing one leaves 1 of 2, which is not a majority, so that is why replica sets use 3 members.

questionText: Rahul sends Aman Rs 500: Rahul -500 and Aman +500, inside one SQL transaction. The server crashes after the first UPDATE, before COMMIT. What is the state after the restart?
option1: Rahul has Rs 500 and Aman has Rs 200: the half-finished transfer stays, so the money is gone
option2: Rahul has Rs 500 and Aman has Rs 700: the database finishes the transfer on its own after restart
option3: The database refuses to start until someone repairs the two balances by hand using backups
option4: Rahul still has Rs 1000 and Aman still has Rs 200: the unfinished transaction is rolled back
correctOptionExplanation: An uncommitted transaction is undone on restart, so the two balances change together or not at all (atomicity).

questionText: The same Rs 500 transfer is written in MongoDB as two separate updateOne calls on two user documents. The server crashes between them. Why can the Rs 500 vanish?
option1: updateOne is not atomic, so only half of the first update was applied before the crash happened, leaving a corrupted document
option2: MongoDB does not support transactions at all, so no operation can ever be undone in any form
option3: MongoDB rolls the first update back, but then forgets to apply the second one after restart
option4: Each updateOne is its own finished write; with no multi-document transaction, the first one is already saved
correctOptionExplanation: A single document is always updated atomically, but two documents are two writes. MongoDB does have multi-document transactions; you must opt in, they cost more, and that is why payments and wallets usually live in SQL.

questionText: The app keeps messages for one year, so all of August 2025 (1,000,000 messages) must go. The SQL table is partitioned by month. What is the fastest way to remove August?
option1: ALTER TABLE messages DROP PARTITION p2025_08, which removes that month as one unit, almost instantly
option2: DELETE FROM messages WHERE sent_at < '2025-09-01', which scans and deletes a million rows one by one and updates every index
option3: TRUNCATE TABLE messages, then restore the other eleven months from a backup afterwards
option4: A cron job that deletes 1,000 rows every minute until the whole month is gone from the table
correctOptionExplanation: Each partition is its own file, so dropping one is cheap and leaves the other months untouched. In MongoDB the months are mixed in one collection: deleteMany removes a million documents one by one and updates every index (a TTL index also deletes one by one).

questionText: Select ALL the true statements about replication, sharding and partitioning.
option1: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several servers (for failover and reads)
option2: Sharding splits the data so each server holds a different part (for size and write scale)
option3: Partitioning splits one table into pieces, usually on the same server
option4: Sharding and partitioning always mean spreading data across servers
option5: Replication makes every server hold a different part of the data
correctOptionExplanation: Replication = copies, sharding = different parts on different servers, partitioning = pieces of one table inside one server. Big systems use all three together.

questionText: A catalog sells phones (ram, battery), shoes (size, colour) and books (pages, author). A product page loads one product at a time. Which design fits best, and why?
option1: One SQL table with a column for every possible attribute: it is the cleanest way to model this
option2: One document per product: each carries only its own fields, and a single read returns the whole page
option3: A SQL table with one row per attribute: rebuilding one product is cheap and needs no extra joins at all
option4: MongoDB is the only possible choice here, because SQL cannot store varying attributes in any form
correctOptionExplanation: A wide SQL table is mostly NULLs, and attributes-as-rows needs many rows per product to rebuild one page. SQL can still do it (for example with a JSON column), so the point is the shape of the data, not that SQL is slow.

questionText: An app records orders, payments and invoices. Every rupee must add up, and one purchase updates several tables at once. What does this favour?
option1: SQL: transactions keep the tables consistent, and constraints reject bad data before it is saved
option2: MongoDB, because documents are always faster than rows, and speed keeps the money consistent
option3: MongoDB, because having no schema means that mistakes in the data cannot happen at all
option4: Neither, because no database can keep several tables consistent while a purchase is running, not even with locks
correctOptionExplanation: Several records that must change together are exactly what transactions are for. That is why real apps keep payments in SQL even when messages live in a NoSQL store.

questionText: Finance asks for total revenue per city for the last 12 months across 50 million orders. Which side is built for this kind of question?
option1: MongoDB, because embedded documents avoid joins, so every report over all orders is cheap
option2: SQL: tables and indexes are made for questions across many records, using GROUP BY and SUM
option3: Neither of them, because values cannot be added up across many rows or documents at once in a reasonable time
option4: Only a cache such as Redis can answer it, because the database is too slow for reports
correctOptionExplanation: A question across many records is SQL's home ground, like Zoya's emoji stats. MongoDB has an aggregation pipeline, but embedding is built for working with one thing at a time.

questionText: A profile page shows the user's name, 5 settings and their 10 latest notifications. All of it is always read together, one user at a time. Which shape fits?
option1: A separate table for each piece, joined at read time, since that is always the fastest option
option2: One document per user that holds name, settings and notifications together, read with a single call
option3: A separate collection for every field, so that each field can be scaled on its own later
option4: It makes no difference: both shapes do exactly the same amount of work for this page
correctOptionExplanation: When you work with one thing as a whole, storing it together means one read. A joined design does the same job with several lookups.

questionText: 50,000 sensors each send a reading every second. Almost every query is "latest readings of sensor X". There are no joins, no shared data, and the volume keeps growing. Which strength matters most here?
option1: Multi-table transactions that update several sensors and their summaries in one step
option2: Foreign keys that tie every reading to its sensor row and reject unknown sensors
option3: Joins that combine readings from many different sensors into one combined result set for each query
option4: Easy sharding for a huge, write-heavy stream of readings with no cross-record queries
correctOptionExplanation: Each sensor can live on its own shard and nothing needs to be joined or updated together, which suits a store with built-in sharding (a time-series database is another good fit).

questionText: Select ALL the situations that favour MongoDB.
option1: Creating, reading and deleting one self-contained thing, such as a message, as a whole
option2: Records whose fields differ by type, such as text, voice and poll messages
option3: Changing a value that is shared by millions of records
option4: Many writers updating the same single item at the same moment
option5: Built-in sharding and automatic failover without extra tooling
correctOptionExplanation: MongoDB shines when one thing is handled as a whole, when shapes differ, and when you need sharding and failover out of the box. Shared values and one hot item are SQL's strengths.

questionText: Select ALL the situations that favour SQL.
option1: A report that asks a question across millions of records
option2: An update that must change three tables together or not at all
option3: Reading one self-contained message together with its reactions in a single call
option4: Changing one shared value that is stored in one place and pointed to by many rows
option5: Adding a brand-new field to every future record without any schema change
correctOptionExplanation: SQL wins when you ask across many things, when several tables must change together (transactions), and when shared data is stored once. The other two are MongoDB's strengths.

questionText: A real chat app uses both kinds of database. Where does each kind of data fit best?
option1: Messages (huge, read as a whole, sharded by chat) in a NoSQL store; users and payments in SQL
option2: Everything in SQL, because NoSQL stores cannot hold chat messages once the app gets any real scale
option3: Everything in MongoDB, because it is always faster than SQL for every kind of data an app holds
option4: Messages in SQL and payments in MongoDB, because payments are naturally shaped like documents
correctOptionExplanation: Pick the database by how you read and write the data. Messages are handled whole and need to be sharded; users are shared and payments need transactions, which fits SQL.

questionText: Orders are sharded by customer_id across servers. The order_items table has no customer_id, so an order's items can land on another server. What is the fix?
option1: Add an index on order_items.order_id, so that the items of one order are found quickly anywhere
option2: Move the orders table to one large server and leave order_items sharded across the others
option3: Copy customer_id into order_items and shard it by customer_id too, so an order and its items sit together
option4: Nothing: a join across servers costs the same as a join on a single server, so no fix is needed
correctOptionExplanation: This is co-location, the same problem as reactions and messages. Every child table needs the shard key, or its rows end up far from their parent.
